title: Sona's strength
hook: the mother of ten who ordained late: effort in old age (Therigatha, Sona)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sumedha talked a king out of a wedding. Your line was she argued her way in. Did you give one clear reason, kindly, when a choice of yours was questioned? Today, a nun who came late, and the strength she found. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

Shame on you, wretched old age. That's how Sona's song ends, and it reads almost like a dare. The path has met her before, in the commentary's story of a late start and a pot of bath water. Today stays with her own verses. She bore ten sons, she says, and by the time she went to a nun to hear the teaching, she was weak and old. No royal refusal, no dramatic escape. A tired body and a decision. Today, the strength she found late.
screen: `SHAME ON YOU, OLD AGE.` → `TODAY, HER OWN VERSES.` → `WEAK AND OLD, SHE GOES.`

segments.voice: First, where she started. Having borne ten sons from this body, she says, weak and old, I went to a nun. She doesn't dress it up. Her strength was gone before her practice began. Second, what she heard. The nun taught her the basics: the heaps that make up a person, the senses, the elements. Sona heard it, cut off her hair, and went forth. Nothing in her verses says she waited to feel stronger first. Third, what she found. Her verses move quickly now. While she trained, she says, the divine eye was made clear, and she came to know her former lives. Her mind became steady and one-pointed. She was freed, clinging to nothing, at peace. The heaps that make up a person, she says, are fully known, and stand now cut off at the root. Fourth, the dare. Then she turns to old age itself. Shame on you, she says, wretched old age; there's no more coming back. Old age had taken her strength of body. It hadn't taken her effort. The strength in the title isn't muscle. In Sona's song it's the will to keep at it, and it didn't wait for her to be young.
screen: `TEN SONS, THEN WEAK AND OLD.` · `SHE HEARS, CUTS HER HAIR, GOES.` · `A STEADY MIND, AND FREED.` · `SHAME ON YOU, OLD AGE.` · then, large: `STRENGTH IN OLD AGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one hard thing to do today, sized to the body you have now. A walk you've been putting off. A phone call. A chore that keeps waiting. Settle first, and let the breath be easy. Picture the hard thing clearly: where you'll be, what the first step is. Notice any voice that says too tired, too old, too late. Don't argue with it. Just let Sona sit beside it, the nun who started weak and old. Then pick a time. The bell holds the time.
Sona's strength. The mother of ten sons who went forth weak and old, was freed, and told old age it had lost. Today's word.
Your line: strength in old age. Today, do the one hard thing you chose, at whatever pace your body allows. Day seven hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, people sometimes ordain or take up serious practice late in life, and Sona's verses are remembered as a sign that effort on the path does not depend on youth.
